text:
NICE guideline NG180, Perioperative care in adults (published August 2020), covers the care of adults undergoing surgery across the preoperative, intraoperative and postoperative periods. It does not replace specialty guidance on venous thromboembolism prophylaxis or antimicrobial prophylaxis, which are covered elsewhere.

Preoperative assessment and optimization. Adults having surgery should have their perioperative risk assessed with a validated risk stratification tool, a clinical assessment before surgery, and a discussion of the assessment, risks and treatment options with their healthcare professional. Each patient should have an identifiable point of contact in the perioperative care team. Adults should be given information and support to reduce modifiable risk factors before surgery (for example smoking cessation and comorbidity optimization).

Preoperative fasting. The committee found sufficient evidence to recommend that patients drink clear fluids until 2 hours before surgery, noting that many patients wrongly believe fluids must be avoided and that clear fluids reduce postoperative headache, nausea and vomiting. Routine preoperative carbohydrate drinks are not recommended for most surgery types. There was a small amount of evidence for reduced thirst and headache, and for reduced length of stay after major abdominal surgery, so carbohydrate drinks may be considered for people having major abdominal surgery. There was no evidence on the optimal timing of carbohydrate drinks.

Managing pain. Patients should be informed of pain management options and actively involved in choosing. Multimodal analgesia was agreed to provide more effective pain relief while reducing opioid need and opioid-related complications. Pre-emptive analgesia should be considered so that pain is managed when local anaesthesia wears off. Paracetamol used alongside opioid analgesia reduces opioid consumption; there was no significant difference in effectiveness between oral and intravenous paracetamol, and intravenous paracetamol is much more expensive, so it is not recommended for people who can take oral medicines. NSAIDs provide effective additional pain relief and reduce the need for other analgesia; traditional NSAIDs are more cost-effective than COX-2 inhibitors, with oral ibuprofen the most cost-effective traditional NSAID, and there was no significant difference between NSAIDs or routes, so intravenous NSAIDs are not recommended for people who can take oral medicines. Opioids remain part of the strategy when needed. For gabapentin, the committee made only a research recommendation on timing and dose for moderate-to-severe expected pain, so no gabapentin dose is recommended in this guideline.

Enhanced recovery and postoperative care. For adults having major or complex elective surgery, an enhanced recovery programme (ERP) spanning the preoperative, intraoperative and postoperative stages is recommended, based on a large body of evidence for shorter stays, fewer complications and lower costs. People with a high risk of complications or mortality should have postoperative care in a non-ward-based specialist recovery area (high-dependency unit, post-anaesthesia care unit or intensive care unit). The WHO surgical safety checklist should be completed for each surgical procedure (reinforced in NICE quality standard QS216).

Limitations. This is a condensed summary of recommendations; for exact recommendation wording, consult the full guideline. Drug doses for analgesics are not specified in the summarized sections; dosing follows product licensing and local formularies.
title: NICE NG180 — Perioperative care in adults
